name: Groove Metal
about: Groove metal was thrash slowed to a mid-tempo swagger. It emerged around 1990 in the American South, where Pantera (and, a few months earlier, New Orleans's Exhorder) traded speed for syncopated, palm-muted riffs that locked to the kick drum, with Dimebag Darrell's squealing harmonics and Phil Anselmo's hardcore bark on top. Vulgar Display of Power in 1992 set the terms, and Sepultura's Chaos A.D. and Machine Head's Burn My Eyes broadened them with tribal percussion and hip-hop-era bounce. The style's emphasis on the riff as rhythm rather than melody fed into nu metal and metalcore, which largely displaced it by 2000, though Lamb of God revived its thrash-schooled form in the 2000s and Gojira gave it an environmentalist, progressive edge. It remains the default sound of American heavy metal radio.

artists.name: Pantera
artists.why: the Texans who defined the style

artists.name: Sepultura
artists.why: Brazilian thrash gone tribal and groovy

artists.name: Chimaira
artists.why: Cleveland's New Wave of American Heavy Metal

artists.name: Gojira
artists.why: French progressive groove with whale-sized riffs

artists.name: Jinjer

albums.title: Vulgar Display of Power
albums.why: Walk, Mouth for War and a new, dry heaviness: the record that replaced thrash with groove as the sound of American metal.

albums.title: Cowboys from Hell
albums.why: The Texans' reinvention after their glam years, with Dimebag's riffs and Anselmo's newly feral voice arriving as if from nowhere.

albums.title: Slaughter in the Vatican
albums.why: Recorded before Cowboys from Hell and released just after, the New Orleans band's debut is the groove-thrash blueprint Pantera got the credit for.

albums.title: Chaos A.D.
albums.why: The Brazilians slowed down, brought in tribal percussion and political fury, and made the decade's most convincing argument that groove could carry a whole album.

albums.title: Burn My Eyes
albums.why: Davidian's opening riff and Robb Flynn's Oakland street rage made Roadrunner's fastest-selling debut and the mid-1990s groove benchmark.

albums.title: Beg to Differ
albums.why: Tommy Victor's clipped, industrial-leaning riffs on the New Yorkers' major-label debut anticipated both groove metal and the 1990s alternative-metal crossover.

albums.title: Cleansing
albums.why: Snap Your Fingers, Snap Your Neck and a Killing Joke bassist gave Prong their tightest, most danceable and most influential record.

albums.title: The Law
albums.why: Slower, groovier and bleaker than the debut, with a Black Sabbath cover that makes the lineage explicit; the band split soon after.

albums.title: Sound of White Noise
albums.why: John Bush's arrival and Dave Jerden's production pulled the thrash veterans into a darker, mid-tempo groove that produced their best-selling album.

albums.title: NOLA
albums.why: Anselmo, Pepper Keenan and Kirk Windstein's side project turned Sabbath, Skynyrd and swamp sludge into a Southern metal classic.

albums.title: Power of Inner Strength
albums.why: Dave Lombardo's post-Slayer band with producer Waldemar Sorychta, a tight and underrated European take on the Pantera formula.

albums.title: Roots
albums.why: Downtuned to the point of collapse and recorded partly with the Xavante people, Roots was both nu metal's midwife and the band's last classic lineup record.

albums.title: Soulfly
albums.why: Max Cavalera's grief-stricken post-Sepultura debut piled tribal drums, guests and dub on the Roots template, with Eye for an Eye its clear peak.

albums.title: The Gathering
albums.why: Dave Lombardo and Steve DiGiorgio join Chuck Billy for a death-tinged groove album that is the Bay Area thrashers' heaviest.

albums.title: The Impossibility of Reason
albums.why: The Cleveland band shed its nu-metal electronics for a thrash-schooled groove record that defined the New Wave of American Heavy Metal.

albums.title: As the Palaces Burn
albums.why: Devin Townsend's production and Chris Adler's drumming turned the Richmond band's groove-thrash into something lean and ferocious.

albums.title: Ashes of the Wake
albums.why: Laid to Rest and Now You've Got Something to Die For made the band's political fury mainstream; the album is the 2000s groove-metal landmark.

albums.title: ...And They Shall Take Up Serpents
albums.why: Appalachian groove metal with progressive detours and a snake-handling concept, the West Virginians' cult classic.

albums.title: The Blackening
albums.why: Ten-minute songs, twin-guitar harmonies and Flynn's most focused anger made the comeback record a late-career landmark and a Grammy nominee.

albums.title: The Last Kind Words
albums.why: Dez Fafara's post-Coal Chamber band at its most melodic and thrashy, with Clouds Over California its signature anthem.

albums.title: Inflikted
albums.why: Max and Igor Cavalera reunited for the first time since Sepultura on a raw, fast groove-thrash album that felt like unfinished business.

albums.title: L'Enfant Sauvage
albums.why: The French band's major-label debut tightened their progressive death metal into groove-driven songs without losing the ecological weight.

albums.title: Magma
albums.why: Written after the Duplantier brothers lost their mother, Magma is shorter, more melodic and more grief-stricken, and brought the band to arenas.

albums.title: King of Everything
albums.why: Tatiana Shmayluk's switches from soulful singing to guttural roars over djent-tinged grooves made the Ukrainians a global live draw.
